us7_israel.topic: Israel: the Rabbinate, personal status law, conversion, burial, Haredi exemptions and funding

claims.text: Ottoman millet system left personal status to religious courts; the British Mandate kept a modified millet system recognising eleven communities (Sunni Islam, Orthodox Judaism, nine Christian denominations); 1947 Ben-Gurion-religious parties 'status quo' agreement left personal status incl. marriage to religious authorities; 1953 rabbinical courts under the Chief Rabbinate given jurisdiction over marriage and divorce of all Jews in Israel; Muslim sharia courts, ten recognised churches, Druze courts (community recognised 1957, courts 1962)

Religious authorities cannot marry interfaith or same-sex couples; non-Orthodox converts not recognised for marriage; kohen may not marry a convert; mamzer restrictions; 2010 Civil Union Law applies only if both partners registered as having no religion; Tzohar Law Oct 2013; get regulation 2016: prosecution for refusal possible only with a rarely used rabbinical-court order; 11,145 Jewish divorces in 2018

1962 Supreme Court: Interior Ministry must register civil marriages performed abroad (registration for statistical purposes); Nov 2006 Barak ruling extended recognition to validity; 2006 Supreme Court 6-1 recognised same-sex marriages performed abroad; CBS: 1,151 same-sex couples registered foreign weddings 2006-2019; ~9,000 couples registered overseas marriages in 2011; CBS identified 9,200 overseas weddings registered in 2022; Lod court Sept 2022 recognised Utah Zoom marriages, Supreme Court upheld 7 March 2023; Hiddush estimate >3,000 couples with an Israeli partner married via Utah by 2024
Hiddush 2013 world map: Israel in 'severe restrictions' group (45 of 194 countries), only democracy in it; 300,000 citizens defined 'without religion' unable to marry in Israel (Hiddush)

Hiddush Jan 2016 report to a Knesset conference: ~660,000 Jewish Israelis cannot legally marry in Israel (364,000 FSU immigrants, 284,000 gays and lesbians, 13,000 non-Orthodox converts); 20% of weddings registered in Israel took place overseas; Hiddush poll: 64% of Jewish Israelis support official recognition of all types of marriage

High Court 1 March 2021, 8-1 (nine-justice panel under Hayut, Sohlberg dissenting on timing): state must recognise Reform and Conservative conversions performed in Israel for the Law of Return; the court had waited ~15 years for legislation; Shas and UTJ condemned it

1996 alternative burial law gives every citizen the right to secular burial funded like Chevra Kadisha burials by National Insurance; 521 local Chevra Kadisha under the Religious Services Ministry; only a handful of secular cemeteries (2016)

Haredi draft timeline: 1948 Torato Umanuto arrangement; 800 exemptions/yr after 1967; 1977 quotas lifted; Tal Law July 2002; 2005 of 41,450 covered only 31 later enlisted; Tal Law struck 21 Feb 2012; enlistment law 12 March 2014; amendments struck 12 Sept 2017; July 2024 3,000 draft notices, fewer than 10% reported; Nov 2024 7,000 more orders and 1,126 arrest warrants; Nov 2025 Bismuth bill: ~80,000 eligible but exempt

High Court 25 June 2024, nine justices unanimous (Vogelman): no legal framework for blanket exemption; state must draft yeshiva students; no state funding for yeshivas and kollels for students without lawful exemption or deferral; 400 exempted in 1949, about 63,000 at end of June 2023

July 2026 law barring arrests of Haredi draft evaders for about seven months frozen by High Court within 24 hours; freeze extended 28 July 2026 by nine-justice panel; AG and Knesset legal adviser urged annulment; government boycotted hearing; ~72,000 Haredi men aged 18-24 eligible had ignored conscription orders

Cabinet approved 10 March 2026 over NIS 5bn ($1.6bn) of coalition funds in the 2026 budget; NIS 2.2bn ($714.8m), 53.19%, for Haredi purposes (Berl Katznelson Center), incl. NIS 1.56bn for Torah institutions (yeshivas and kollels), NIS 75m recognised-but-unofficial schools, NIS 32m exempt schools; Finance Ministry reportedly opposed; coalition funds peaked at NIS 5.5bn in 2024

IDI 2025: Haredi population ~750,000 (10%) in 2009, ~948,000 (11%) in 2015, 1,452,350 (14.3%) in 2025; male employment roughly one-third c.2002, 52% 2015, ~54% latest, stalled since 2016; yeshiva and kollel students 169,366 in 2023, +83% since 2013; 2,560 entered military and 500 civilian service in 2024; 3,060 in 2025 vs 3,022 in 2015
IDI 2025 (as reported): 33% of Haredi families below the poverty line vs 14% of non-Haredi Jewish families; bagrut eligibility 10% to 16% over the decade vs ~85% in state and state-religious streams
Pew GRI (0-10): Israel 3.9 (year to June 2007) and 6.7 (2022); US 1.6 and 2.7; SHI Israel 7.8 and 7.1, US 1.9 and 1.3
Pew 18 Dec 2024: Israel's GRI rose from 5.7 to 6.7 in 2022, into 'very high' (6.6-10.0); 'high' is 4.5-6.5

us7_us.topic: United States: separation of church and state, religious exemptions, funding of religious schools, civil marriage

claims.text: First Amendment (ratified Dec 1791): 'Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof'; Everson v. Board of Education (1947, Black): upheld NJ bus-fare funding for parochial pupils, invoked Jefferson's 'wall of separation', incorporated the clause against the states; Lemon v. Kurtzman (1971) struck Pennsylvania aid to religious schools, three-part test; Zelman v. Simmons-Harris (2002) upheld vouchers
Kennedy v. Bremerton, 27 June 2022, 6-3 (Gorsuch): protected a coach's personal prayer; abandoned the Lemon test for a history-based approach; Groff v. DeJoy (2023) called Lemon 'now abrogated'

Employment Division v. Smith (1990): neutral generally applicable laws need not meet strict scrutiny; RFRA (1993) restored strict scrutiny (compelling interest, least restrictive means); Burwell v. Hobby Lobby, 30 June 2014, 5-4 (Alito): contraceptive mandate violated RFRA for closely held for-profit corporations

Trinity Lutheran (2017) barred excluding a church school from a playground grant; Espinoza (2020) barred excluding religious schools from a state scholarship programme; Carson v. Makin, 21 June 2022, 6-3: Maine's nonsectarian requirement violated Free Exercise; Roberts: exclusion 'promotes stricter separation of church and state than the Federal Constitution requires'

Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board v. Drummond, 22 May 2025: 4-4 (Barrett recused) affirmed Oklahoma Supreme Court barring public funds to St. Isidore religious charter school; no nationwide precedent
Obergefell v. Hodges, 26 June 2015, 5-4: states must license and recognise same-sex marriages; Respect for Marriage Act signed 13 Dec 2022; Court declined Kim Davis petition to overturn Obergefell
Pew RLS: Christians 78% (2007), 71% (2014), 62% (2023-24); religiously unaffiliated 16%, 23%, 29%; non-Christian religions 4.7% (2007) to 7.1%; Jewish 1.7%, Muslim 1.2% (2023-24)
EdChoice: ~10,000 students in private school choice programmes in 1996; ~540,545 in 2019; passed one million in 2024; Arizona ESA universal 2022
EdChoice Dec 2025: more than 1.5 million students in 75 private school choice programmes in 34 states plus DC and Puerto Rico; eight states enacted or expanded programmes in 2025

One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed 4 July 2025 created the federal Education Freedom Tax Credit, effective 1 Jan 2027; 31 states opted in or announced intent by 28 July 2026; ~51.7m of 56.4m students expected eligible (up to 300% of area median income)

Johnson Amendment (1954) in section 501(c)(3) bars churches and other 501(c)(3)s from endorsing or opposing candidates; in National Religious Broadcasters v. Commissioner (E.D. Tex.) the IRS joined a motion for a consent judgment barring enforcement against the plaintiff churches for speech to congregations through customary channels; required the judge's approval

Consent judgment filed 7 July 2025; IRS acknowledged good-faith speech to a congregation during religious services is not campaign intervention; settlement does not remove the Johnson Amendment from law
